slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can summarise records by group, which is a PivotTable written as code, and lay the result out as a grid. You can merge two tables on a join key, say which rows each kind of join keeps, and prove with a row count and with the validate option that no rows were lost and none were multiplied.

And you can pull months and weekdays out of a date and report revenue by branch, region and year. All of it runs on the Lakeside Mart files in a Google Colab notebook.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Word
What it means
groupby and aggregation
Split records into groups by a key, then reduce each group to one number, such as a sum or a mean.
Merge (join) and join key
Combine two tables by matching a shared variable. The join type says which unmatched records survive.
Cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-one)
How many records on each side match one key value. It decides if a merge keeps, loses or multiplies rows.
Fan-out (row multiplication) and lost rows
Fan-out: a merge repeats a record, so totals inflate. Lost rows: records with no match that an inner join drops.
pivot_table (wide and long format)
A summary grid with one variable down the side and one across the top, which is wide format.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

groupby and aggregation. Split records into groups by a key, then reduce each group to one number, such as a sum or a mean.

Merge (join) and join key. Combine two tables by matching a shared variable. The join type says which unmatched records survive.

Cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-one). How many records on each side match one key value. It decides if a merge keeps, loses or multiplies rows.

Fan-out (row multiplication) and lost rows. Fan-out: a merge repeats a record, so totals inflate. Lost rows: records with no match that an inner join drops.

pivot_table (wide and long format). A summary grid with one variable down the side and one across the top, which is wide format.

title.text:
groupby splits the records into groups
and reduces each group to one number

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_split_apply_11.90x4.25_c3c620b8.png
objects.alt: groupby splits the records into groups and reduces each group to one number

objects.text: An excerpt of six orders. Colours mark the groups. An aggregation turns many values into one.

slides.notes:
This is groupby, in three steps: split, apply, combine. On the left are six real orders from the Lakeside orders file, with the branch and the order value. Step one splits them into one pile per branch. Step two applies an aggregation to each pile, here a sum, which turns many values into one.

Step three combines the answers into a small table with one record per group. In Excel you do the same when you drag branch to the rows box of a PivotTable and the value to the values box. The numbers here are only for these six orders. How many records come back when you group by branch?

slides.notes:
You already know every one of these tools from Excel, so here is the translation. The rows box of a PivotTable is the grouping key in groupby. The values box, with Sum, Count or Average, is an aggregation. VLOOKUP becomes merge, which is a join on a join key.

A lookup column next to your whole list, where the missing ones show blank, is a left join. And a PivotTable with a field across the top is a pivot table in wide format. The pandas names are the real function names, so you will see them in documentation, in tests at interviews and in other people's notebooks.

Which row do you use most in Excel today?

title.text:
Named aggregation gives several
answers per group in one step

runs.text: # orders.csv is already loaded as orders

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: groupby names the variable that makes the groups: one group per branch.
Each line inside agg is a new column: its name, then the variable and the aggregate function.
Branch B01 has 5,885 orders and revenue of UGX 283,331,305.
These totals describe the 5 percent sample of till orders in the file.

slides.notes:
Usually one number per group is not enough. A manager wants the count of orders, the revenue and the average order, side by side. In pandas that is agg with named aggregation. Each line inside agg makes one new column: the name you choose, then in brackets the variable and the aggregate function.

The result has one record per branch and three variables. Branch B01 has 5,885 orders, revenue of 283,331,305 shillings and an average order of about 48,145. All of these figures describe only the sample of till orders in the file. Which aggregate function would you add to see the largest order?

title.text:
count skips missing values
and size counts every record

objects.text:
records  filled
branch_id
B01           5885    4071
B02           4830    3370
B03           3345    2336
In plain words

runs.text: size counts the records in each group, filled or not.
count counts only the filled values of one variable. Walk-in orders have a missing customer_id, so filled is smaller.
In B01: 5,885 records but 4,071 filled customer_id values.
Say which you mean before you report a number of orders.

slides.notes:
A small trap in aggregation. Size counts the records in each group. Count counts only the values that are filled in for one variable. In branch B01 there are 5,885 orders, but only 4,071 of them have a customer id, because the others are walk-in shoppers with a missing value.

So if you count customer ids you get a smaller number than if you count orders, and nothing warns you. Decide what you are counting, records or filled values, and use size or count to match. Which one would you use for the number of orders?

title.text:
VLOOKUP returns the first match
and merge returns every match

objects.text: VLOOKUP in Sheets

runs.text: Finds the first match and stops.
Fills one helper column at a time.

objects.text: merge in pandas

runs.text: Returns every match, one row per pair.
Adds all the variables you pick in one line.

objects.text: Returning every match is useful, and it means the row count can change.

slides.notes:
The second big idea today is bringing information in from another table, which is the job you give to VLOOKUP. VLOOKUP looks for your key in a second table and returns the first match, then stops. You also fill one helper column at a time. In pandas the function is merge.

It adds every variable you ask for in one line, and it does not stop at the first match. It returns every match. When a key is not found, VLOOKUP shows hash N slash A, and pandas leaves NaN. Read the verdict. Returning every match is the whole power of a merge, and it is also why the row count can change under you.

Have you ever seen a VLOOKUP list grow?

title.text:
A join type decides which
records without a match survive

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_join_types_11.90x4.25_5c8e9cba.png
objects.alt: A join type decides which records without a match survive

objects.text: A real excerpt, joined on customer_id. Gold cells are NaN (missing).

slides.notes:
Here are the four join types, on a real excerpt. The left table has three orders. One of them is a walk-in with no customer id. The right table has three customers, and one of them has no order in the excerpt. An inner join keeps only the keys found in both tables, so two rows.

A left join keeps every order, and the walk-in gets NaN for the loyalty tier. A right join keeps every customer, so the customer without an order appears with NaN for the order. And a full outer join keeps everything, four rows. In practice you will use left and inner joins most.

Which one would you use to list every order with its customer details?

title.text:
An inner join to customers loses
9,171 orders, the walk-in sales

objects.text: of the 30,229 orders have no customer_id. An inner join with customers keeps 21,058 rows. The 9,171 lost rows hold UGX 436,795,845 of revenue.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_8ec48331.png
objects.alt: An inner join to customers loses 9,171 orders, the walk-in sales

slides.notes:
Now the first way a merge goes wrong without an error message: lost rows. The orders file has 30,229 orders. Of those, 9,171 have no customer id, because the shopper was a walk-in. If you inner join orders to customers, those orders have no match, so they disappear.

You keep 21,058 rows. The lost rows are about 30 in every 100 orders, and they hold 436,795,845 shillings of revenue. Your report would say revenue is lower than the tills say, and nothing would warn you. The fix is a left join and a row count. Which join would you choose to keep every order?

title.text:
Cardinality tells you in advance whether
a merge keeps, loses or multiplies rows

rows.text: Cardinality
Lakeside example
What happens to the row count
many-to-one (m:1)
orders to branches on branch_id: each branch appears once.
Safe. Every order keeps one row: 30,229 stays 30,229.
one-to-many (1:m)
orders to order_lines on order_id: about 3.2 lines per order.
Fan-out. 30,229 orders become 98,066 rows.
many-to-many (m:m)
order_lines to returns on order_id: both sides repeat the key.
Rows multiply: the lines of a returned order meet each of its returns. An inner join gives 10,801 rows, about 5 times the 2,056 returns. Join on order_id and product_id.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bag_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

objects.text: Check first: is the join key unique on each side? A key that is unique on one side only is one-to-many.

slides.notes:
Cardinality is how many records on each side match one key value, and it tells you in advance what a merge will do. Merge orders to branches on branch id. Each branch appears once on the right, so this is many-to-one, and every order keeps exactly one row.

Merge orders to order lines on order id. One order has about 3.2 lines, so this is one-to-many, and 30,229 orders become 98,066 rows. That is fan-out. Merge order lines to returns on order id and both sides repeat the key. That is many-to-many. The lines of each returned order meet each of its returns, so you get 10,801 rows, about 5 times the 2,056 returns.

The fix is to join on order id and product id. Before any merge, ask whether the key is unique on each side.

title.text:
Fan-out repeats the order value on every
line, so a sum counts it several times

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_fanout_7.70x4.80_91c617ca.png
objects.alt: Fan-out repeats the order value on every line, so a sum counts it several times

objects.text: Fan-out (row multiplication): a one-to-many merge repeats the left record once for every match.

runs.text: Order O000006 has 3 lines, so it becomes 3 rows.
order_value_ugx belongs to the whole order, so adding it up now counts it once per line.

slides.notes:
Here is fan-out, also called row multiplication, on one real order. Order O000006 is one record in the orders table, with an order value of 44,900 shillings. It has 3 records in the order lines table. When you merge on order id, the order record is repeated once for each line, so you get 3 rows.

The order value is a fact about the whole order, so it is now written 3 times. If you add up that variable, you get 134,700, which is 3 times the real 44,900. The merge ran without any error. How would you notice, if you did not look at the row count?

title.text:
On the full file, fan-out makes
revenue 5.3 times too big

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_d0c2738b.png
objects.alt: On the full file, fan-out makes revenue 5.3 times too big

objects.text: 30,229 orders became 98,066 rows after the merge.

runs.text: Ratio 5.3, above the 3.2 times rows grew: big orders have more lines.

slides.notes:
Now the same mistake on the whole orders file. The true revenue is 1,435.6 million shillings. After merging orders to order lines and adding up the order value, the total is 7,606.1 million. That is 5.3 times too big. Look at the number of rows: 30,229 orders became 98,066 rows.

Rows grew 3.2 times, but the revenue grew 5.3 times, because big orders have more lines, so they are repeated more often. A manager who saw the bigger figure might celebrate. Which check would have caught this at once?

title.text:
validate='m:1' makes pandas stop
a merge that is not many-to-one

runs.text: # orders and lines are already loaded

objects.text:
Merge keys are not unique in right dataset
not a many-to-one merge
In plain words

runs.text: validate states the cardinality you expect: m:1 is many-to-one.
order_lines repeats order_id, so the right side is not unique and pandas raises a MergeError.
The merge never runs, so the revenue cannot inflate.

slides.notes:
Here is the best protection. When you merge, tell pandas what cardinality you expect with the validate option. Here we ask for many-to-one, which means the key must be unique in the right table. But order lines repeats the order id, so the right table is not unique.

pandas stops with a MergeError and a message that says the merge keys are not unique in the right dataset. The merge never runs. The other values you can give are one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many. Make validate a habit on every merge, because it turns a silent mistake into a loud one.

Where in your own work would a loud error be better than a quiet wrong number?

title.text: Four checks around every merge protect the total

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_2bea8746.png
objects.alt: Four checks around every merge protect the total

objects.text: Join log (an audit trail for merges): a small table with the step, rows before, rows after and a note, like the data cleaning log. A change you cannot explain is a stop sign.

slides.notes:
These are the four checks to run around every merge. One, check the key: is it unique on each side, and what is the cardinality?

Two, write down the row count before. Three, merge with an explicit how and with validate, so pandas can refuse a merge that is not what you expected. Four, compare the row count after, and compare the total of a variable that must not change. Keep the counts in a join log.

That is an audit trail for merges: a small table with the step, the rows before, the rows after and a note, just like the data cleaning log from Session 8. A change you cannot explain is a stop sign. Which check do you think people skip most often?

title.text:
A safe lookup: many-to-one, left
join, row counts before and after

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: how=left keeps every order. validate says the join key must be unique in branches.
The printed line shows the count before, the count after and whether they are equal.
30,229 orders in, 30,229 rows out: nothing lost, nothing multiplied.
Add a line to your join log every time.

slides.notes:
Here is the safe pattern for a lookup. Merge orders to branches with how equal to left and validate many-to-one. Before the merge we store the row count. After the merge we print the count before, the count after and whether the two are equal. Both counts are 30,229, so nothing was lost and nothing was multiplied.

This is the line you copy into your join log. Many-to-one with a left join is the standard way to add names, categories and regions to a table of events. What would the output show if two branches had the same branch id?

title.text:
To use the many side, summarise
it first and then merge one-to-one

objects.text: 30229 True
In plain words

runs.text: groupby reduces the lines to one record per order, with the number of lines and their total.
validate='1:1' confirms the key is unique on both sides.
30,229 rows come out. The total of the lines equals the total of the orders: True. The == test is safe here because both totals are whole shillings; with decimals use abs(a - b) < 0.01.
The pattern: summarise the many side, then merge.

slides.notes:
And when you do need information from the many side, such as the number of lines on each order, first reduce the lines to one record per order with groupby. Then merge one-to-one. The row count stays at 30,229, and the total of the line revenue equals the total of the order values, which prints True.

That second check is a reconciliation: two totals that should agree do agree. The pattern is simple to remember: summarise the many side first, then merge. What would you put in the summary if you needed the largest line on each order?

title.text:
Convert text to a datetime first,
and then read its parts with .dt

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_datetime_parts_11.90x4.25_eaac39c5.png
objects.alt: Convert text to a datetime first, and then read its parts with .dt

objects.text: Order O000006 was placed on 2024-01-03. dayofweek counts Monday as 0.

slides.notes:
The last topic is dates. In Session 8 you saw that dates arrive as text. Step one is pd.to_datetime, which turns the text into a real datetime. Then the dot dt gives you the parts. For order O000006, placed on 2024-01-03, the year is 2024, the month is 1, the day is 3, and the weekday name is Wednesday.

Day of week as a number counts Monday as zero. Text has no month or weekday, and it sorts alphabetically, so a month taken from text is a guess. With a month and a weekday you can group revenue by them. Which part would you group by to compare months?

title.text:
Revenue by weekday: derive the part,
group by it, then put it in calendar order

objects.text: Thursday 223743120
In plain words

runs.text: orders is already loaded. dt.day_name() gives the weekday name of each order.
groupby adds up the order value for each weekday.
reindex puts the rows in calendar order, Monday first. Without it they sort alphabetically.
idxmax gives the weekday with the largest total. max gives the total.

slides.notes:
Here is revenue by weekday. We turn the date into a datetime, take the weekday name, group by it and add up the order value. Then reindex puts the rows in calendar order, because otherwise groupby sorts them alphabetically. The last line asks which weekday has the largest total.

The answer is Thursday, with 223,743,120 shillings. The picture after this shows all seven days. Notice that the date conversion is the first line. Without it nothing else works. Which other part of a date could you group by?

objects.text: Revenue of three branches by year. The numbers are the same in both layouts.

slides.notes:
Reshaping means changing the layout of the same numbers. In long format, there is one record for each branch and year, so the year is a value in a column. In wide format there is one record for each branch, and each year has its own column. pivot_table goes from long to wide, and melt goes back from wide to long.

Long format is what groupby returns and what most chart tools want. Wide format is easier for people to read, and it is what a PivotTable shows. The revenue numbers are identical, only the year moves between a row value and a column heading. You will use both layouts in your course project.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: What you see
What it means
What to do
A row count after the merge is bigger than before
The right table repeats the key: fan-out.
Add validate='m:1'. Find which key repeats. Summarise the right table first.
KeyError: 'branch_name'
The variable is not in the table you are using.
Print the column names with .columns and check the spelling.
MergeError: not a many-to-one merge
That is validate working correctly.
Read the message. Decide whether the merge is wrong or the expectation is.
Weekday rows are in alphabetical order
groupby sorts the keys.
Add .reindex with the list of weekday names.
Totals double after running a cell twice
The cell merged into a table that was already merged.
Rerun from the cell that loads the files.

Five messages and symptoms you may meet. A row count bigger after the merge means the right table repeats the key, so add validate and summarise the right side first. A KeyError for a variable name means the variable is not in the table you are using, so print the column names.

A MergeError that says not a many-to-one merge is validate doing its job, so read it before you silence it. Weekdays in alphabetical order need reindex. And totals that double after you run a cell twice mean you merged into a table that was already merged, so rerun from the loading cell. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

Short answer
Order O000006 has 3 lines and an order value of 44,900. What do you get when you add up order_value_ugx after merging orders to order_lines?
134,700, which is 3 times too big, because the order value is repeated on each of the 3 rows.

A left join from orders to customers. It keeps every order, including walk-ins, who get NaN for the tier.
Which option makes pandas refuse a merge where the right table repeats the key?
validate='m:1' (many-to-one). It raises a MergeError before the merge runs.
